A R T I C L E I N F O   
Keywords: 
Machine learning 
Deep learning 
Procedural content generation 
Image generation 
Games 
A B S T R A C T   
Modern games are among the most intricate pieces of software ever devised. However, artists have little to no 
means of porting their creative work from title to title as the aesthetics change and older models grow to look 
obsolete. Zooming into the topic of assisted game art generation, the literature is notably scarce, although ad­
vances towards automated asset generation are of paramount interest to the field. In this work, we investigate the 
use of deep learning algorithms to create pixel art sprites from line art sketches to produce artwork of sufficient 
quality to be used within a game product with little to no manual editing by human artists. Such a problem 
contrasts with well-known tasks studied in the literature, which are based on natural pictures, boast massive 
datasets, and are much more tolerant to noise. In addition, we conducted a case study of applying current 
technology to the drawing pipeline of an upcoming game title, attaining useful and positive results that may fast- 
track the game development, supporting the argument that current image generation state-of-the-art is ready to 
be used in some real-world tasks.   
1. Introduction 
Designing games is a profound technical and artistic challenge [1]. 
Modern games are among the most intricate pieces of software ever 
devised, touching almost every field of computer science while featuring 
thousands of intricate models, high-resolution textures, skeletal ani­
mations, and complex soundtracks [2]. To cope with the ever-growing 
complexity, developers decouple the needed infrastructure as an “en­
gine”, which can be developed independently and shared among several 
titles [3]. On the other hand, artists have little to no means of porting 
their work from title to title, as the aesthetics change and older models 
grow to look obsolete. In this regard, advances towards assisted or 
automated asset generation are of paramount interest to the field. 
Artistic work, within games, range from conceptualizing the game 
and its mechanics to painting textures and sprites, creating visual 
models and their animations, composing the soundtrack, and writing 
down dialogues. Collectively, these elements are known as the game’s 
content, and the automation of such tasks is known as Procedural 
Content Generation (PCG) [4–6]. This field draws methods from a wide 
range of disciplines, such as graph theory, image processing, physics, AI, 
and natural language processing. A recent survey on the topic is 
presented by Liu et al. [7]. 
Since 2012, with the debut of AlexNet [8], the computer vision 
community strode greatly in how well computers can parse and generate 
images. For the first time, computers became able to generate realisti­
cally looking images out of nowhere [9–11]. Critically, we wonder: Is the 
current state-of-the-art in image generation usable to generate 2D content in 
lieu of human artists? Or, more generally, can vision models be effectively 
used to reduce iteration times for asset production?. 
To explore this inquiry, we considered Trajes Fatais: Suits of Fate, a 2D 
pixel-art fighting game inspired by the late nineties classics of the genre. 
In particular, we investigate drawing character sprites from rough line- 
art sketches using neural networks [12]. Concretely, each character has 
an average of 508 sprites, which are drawn as two independent sub- 
sprites, one dedicated to shading and the other to coloring, as shown 
in Fig. 1. Using deep learning [13], we train models to translate line-art 
sketches into each of these sub-sprites, striving to generate content that 
can be polished/accepted by a human artist in less time than it would 
take to draw the asset from scratch. 
This work extends our previous inquiry on the topic, which evaluated 
the Pix2Pix [14] architecture as a means to translate sketches into usable 
artwork [15], obtaining moderately successful results. In summary,

regressing shading values worked remarkably well, outputting similar

adequately inferred by the algorithm, yielding noisy/blurred images. 
Additionally, the algorithm performed poorly on challenging poses for 
both tasks and, especially for the coloring problem, quantizing the 
continuous color range to the set of allowed colors introduced signifi­
cant artifacts. 
In this paper, we propose a radically different approach based on 
casting the problem as a per-pixel classification task using a combination 
of the U-Net architecture [16,17], dense connections [18], focal loss 
[19], class weighting [20] and multi-level supervision [21], while 
removing the discriminator and adversarial training components [14]. 
In our experiments, we obtained vastly improved results for both 
shading and coloring problems while solving many of the shortcomings 
of the previous implementation. Also, qualitatively, the game’s art team 
reported that many of the new generated sprites are almost ready to be 
used on real game production, with little to no manual editing. Code and 
data available at https://github.com/nuzrub/PaintingGameAssetsWith 
DeepLearning. 
2. Related work 
Since the debut of GANs in 2014 [10], the image generation field has 
made significant advances. In its earlier years, authors tackled stable 
training and mode collapse [22–24]. By 2017, realistically looking high- 
resolution portraits could be generated [25], soon followed by GANs 
that can reproduce most classes in ImageNet [26] and models that allow 
some degree of artistic control [11,27,28]. Closely related, models for 
style transfer [29], image colorization [30], domain translation [14,31], 
super-resolution [32,33] and image interpolation were also proposed 
[34,35]. In parallel, while these works address natural images, several 
authors have devoted their time to other visual styles, such as cartoon 
[36,37] and anime images [38,39]. 
While GANs dominate most of the earlier literature, other ap­
proaches have gained traction in later years. Most noticeably, varia­
tional auto-encoders (VAEs) [9,40] and auto-regressive models [41–43]. 
While GANs avoid a direct probabilistic formulation, VAEs explicitly 
model the dataset probability distribution and learn to sample it to 
generate new images. In turn, auto-regressive models generate images 
one pixel at a time by sampling a learned probability distribution and 
conditioning it to all previously generated pixels. Besides formulation 
innovations, many authors are exploring the use of Attention/Trans­
former based architectures within the image generation context 
[44–46]. 
At large, generative models can be divided into fully unsupervised/ 
weakly supervised approaches, which generate images primarily from 
noise/labels [11,26,27,42], and strongly supervised methods, which 
start from an input image that strongly conditions the final output 
[14,30,31,34,35]. The latter is of special interest to asset generation as it 
allows a greater degree of artistic control. In addition, model training is 
considerably less resource-intensive [14] when input–output pairs are 
available than when there are only unpaired samples [31]. 
Zooming into the topic of game art generation, the literature is 
notably scarce [4,6,7]. To the best of our knowledge, only a few authors 
have tackled the automatic sprite generation problem. Horsley et al. 
attempted to generate 8-bit sprites from random noise using a simple 
GAN model, achieving limited results [47]. Concurrently, Xue et al. 
sought to generate plausible next-frame sprites for a given animation 
sequence using a probabilistic CNN model [35]. More recently, Hong 
et al. proposed a multi-discriminator GAN to generate novel sprites from 
a set of shape, color and animation cues. Tackling the problem in the 
opposite direction, Smirnov et al. proposed a model to extract sprites 
from game scenes [48]. Beyond sprite generation, most deep learning 
works within PCG are dedicated to 2D or 3D level generation [5–7,49]. 
We attribute the scarcity of published works dealing with automatic 
sprite generation and, more specifically, character design, to the amount 
of detail involved and the importance of such assets. Poorly generated 
characters would be readily noticed by users, negatively impacting the 
overall game experience. In this context, it remains open whether cur­
rent approaches are ready to solve real-world tasks, which often (1) lack 
large datasets, (2) deviate considerably from natural images, and (3) are 
extremely intolerant to errors and artifacts of any kind. 
This work’s main contribution to state-of-the-art image generation is 
a resounding yes to this open question. To reach this conclusion, we 
conducted a case study of applying current technology to the drawing 
pipeline of an upcoming game title, named Trajes Fatais: Suits of Fate, 
attaining useful results that may fast-track the game development. Such 
a problem contrasts with well-known tasks studied in the literature 
[11,26,42,50], which are based on natural pictures, boast massive 
datasets, and are much more tolerant to noise. 
3. The sprite creation pipeline 
In Trajes Fatais: Suits of Fate, the art director creates every sprite as a 
rough sketch to test the animation ideas. After this initial step, these 
sketches are redrawn as line-art mock-ups and are handed over to the 
drawing team to be completed. Fig. 2 shows two sprites at their early 
sketch stage. This pipeline centers the characters’ design around the art 
director while delegating the creative drawing to the other artists. On 
average, artists take less than two minutes to draw initial sketches and 
no more than ten minutes to draw their line-art counterparts. 
To replicate the late nineties look, each character is limited to 252 
colors. To effectively use this palette in a meaningful way, each sprite is 
drawn twice: as a shading sprite and as a coloring one. The former uses 
up to 6 gray tones to convey the shading information and, the latter, up 
to 42 different colors to mark the different regions of the sprite, such as 
hair, skin, clothes, accessories, etc. Combined, these two sprites identify

up to 6 ∗42 = 252 unique areas, which are encoded as a final sprite. In 
game, each shading-color pair is assigned a color from a palette, creating 
the character’s final look, as shown in Fig. 1. This procedure streamlines 
the artist’s work as it relaxes the 252 color limitation into two distinct 
and intuitive tasks. Fig. 3 shows the shading and coloring sprites of three 
characters in their idle pose. 
Of all stages, drawing shading sprites is the most time-consuming 
step, taking anywhere from 30 to 90 min to be completed, as shading 
complexity varies significantly across characters due to clothing, hair, 
and muscles. On the other hand, drawing the color sprites is consider­
ably easier, as the task is mainly to label each region with its associated 
color. These sprites take at most 15 min to be completed, with most of 
this time being devoted to fine features, such as the eyes, lips, and 
accessories. 
Finally, it is noteworthy to mention that, although 42 individual 
coloring tones can be used, most characters employ less than the 
maximum set of tones. On average, each character uses 37 tones, with 
the least using only 24. Moreover, some of these tones are assigned to 
effects, never being used on the character itself. 
4. Deep-learning asset generation 
The problem of converting line-art sketches into shading and color­
ing sprites is essentially a semantic segmentation problem, in which 
every pixel has to be labeled among one of 6 shadings and 42 coloring 
tones, respectively. In our previous work, we approached the problem 
using the Pix2Pix architecture [14], which learns to regress each pixel to 
the target tone under an adversarial learning setting [10]. Among the 
shortcomings of this approach, the algorithm is biased towards the 
average tone, and the final output has to be quantized to the set of 
allowed colors. 
On top of the aforementioned issues, we also highlight that both 
tasks have class imbalance issues. On shading sprites, the sixth tone (the 
highlight) is sparingly used in relation to the others. On coloring sprites, 
labels such as the eyes and lips occupy a minor fraction of the entire 
sprite while others such as the legs and arms dominate most of the 
image. For that reason, techniques to balance each tone’s importance 
are of paramount significance to this problem. 
Finally, it is noteworthy to mention that, artistically, not all errors 
are valued the same. For instance, mistaking the sixth shading tone 
(highlight) with the fifth (bright) is less of an error than mistaking it with 
the first (darkest tone). Likewise, painting the eye region with the face 
tone is more acceptable than painting it with the leg color. 
To address each of these issues, we combined several deep learning 
techniques into a custom-tailored model. First, we base ourselves on the 
U-Net architecture [16], which is the encoder-decoder model that 
powers most semantic segmentation networks. Second, we elaborate the 
downsampling and upsampling steps using dense connections [18], 
similarly to the Multi-Resolution U-Net model [17]. Third, in a similar 
style to the U-Net 3 + network [21], we employ deep supervision to 
regularize our model. And, finally, regarding our loss function, we 
employ the focal loss function [19] weighted by the effective number of 
samples of each class [20], addressing the class imbalance issues. Fig. 4 
shows an overview of all these elements. In the following subsections, 
We elaborate on each of these elements. 
4.1. U-Net architecture 
Our network design originates from the famous U-Net architecture, 
which consists of an encoder-decoder model with skip connections be­
tween the encoder and decoder layers [16,51]. The encoder is a neural 
network that progressively down-samples the input while increasing the 
number of dimensions, effectively converting spatial information into 
semantic features. In the opposite direction, the decoder distills the 
learned semantics back into the spatial domain, progressively up- 
sampling the input while lowering the number of dimensions. In- 
between, the output of each encoder step is also fed to the respective 
decoder step, creating a skip-connection. 
Among these elements, the skip-connection is the highlight of this 
architecture. In practice, connecting the decoder steps with the raw 
encoder outputs allows the network to recall low-level features directly, 
such as shapes and edges, instead of encoding these elements along with 
the semantic features. Additionally, it greatly improves the gradient 
flow within the model, as gradients can flow uninterrupted from one 
side to the other. 
In our case, we developed the architecture to input and output 256 ×
256 pixels images in one-hot encoding [51] using 7 down/up-sampling 
steps. Input line-art sketches have 3 possible labels: background, 
silhouette, and fill; shading sprites have 7 possible labels, six shading 
tones, and a dedicated background class; and, likewise, coloring sprites 
can have up to 42 color labels plus an additional background class. 
4.2. Dense connections 
The original U-Net model employs two convolution operations per 
down-sampling step and three for each up-sampling one. To allow the 
model to explore the input space further, more layers are needed. 
However, this can quickly escalate to prohibitive proportions. To bal­
ance network depth with resource usage, we resort to dense connections 
[18] similarly to the work of Ibtehaz and Rahman [17]. 
At a high level, given a convolution with f filters, a dense block 
factors this operation into n sequential convolutions with f/n filters. 
Then, the outputs of each intermediate convolution are concatenated to 
compose a tensor with f channels. Finally, to improve gradient flow, a 
residual connection is added, summing the original input with the final 
concatenated features, using a 1 × 1 convolution to equate the number 
of dimensions, if necessary. This process is shown in Fig. 5. 
In practice, this also reduces the number of parameters used by the 
network. While a single s × s convolution operating over f input filters 
and generating f output filters requires p = s2f2 parameters, the

4.3. Dense supervision 
Traditionally, the input image is used solely as the first layer of the 
network and only the last layer’s results are compared to the ground 
truth. Dense supervision breaks this tradition by appending a down- 
sampled version of the input at each down-sampling step and super­
vising the output of each up-sampling step using a down-sampled 
version of the output, effectively supervising the model across every 
scale [21]. 
In our work, the benefit of using dense supervision is the automatic 
creation of smooth labels to regularize the network. Since we use one- 
hot encoding at the input and output level, this forces the algorithm to 
understand which tones are more prevalent within each region and 
which tones go together more often. Ultimately, this greatly reduces the 
number of blatant errors, such as mistaking the eye label for the leg 
label, since these two tones rarely appear around the same areas. 
Care must be taken, however, to ensure the algorithm will prioritize 
the last layer, which is the output we are really interested in. For that, we 
weight the seven computed losses (L ) independently, while ensuring 
the total weight distribution averages to one. Concretely, the highest 
resolution output is given half of the total weight and each subsequent 
output is given half of the remainder, as shown below:

4.4. Class-weighted focal loss 
Given the task of classifying each pixel as one of many labels, we 
follow the traditional choice of using the softmax activation in each 
output layer along with the categorical cross-entropy loss [51]. To 
improve performance, we augment this loss with a focal term [19], 
which down-weights each pixel proportionally to the γ-power of the 
algorithm confidence. Therefore, this term gradually shifts the algo­
rithm attention from well-classified pixels to yet unsure ones. This also 
counteracts class imbalance, as majority classes tend to be learned first 
and, as the training progresses, are gradually down-weighted, shifting 
the algorithm’s attention to the minority classes. 
To further cope with imbalance issues, we also include class weights 
based on the effective number of samples of each class [20]. The ratio­
nale for this term is that the net benefit of more samples diminishes as 
more samples are added, thus, this phenomenon must be accounted for 
when weighting classes to avoid over-penalization. The formula for the 
effective number of samples of a class with n samples is given as 
(1 −βn)/(1 −β), with β ∈[0, 1[. To include this term in the loss formu­
lation, the class weights are normalized, so they average to one, and 
their inverse is multiplied with the loss term. 
Some severely underrepresented labels were assigned large weights 
in our specific case, pushing all other label weights down due to 
normalization. This had the adverse effect of slowing down training, as 
these labels appear infrequently. To counter this effect, we artificially 
added k = 32.768 to n when calculating the effective number of samples 
of each class, smoothing weights more evenly among all labels. 
Putting it all together, our complete loss formulation is given as the 
sum of the weighted focal cross-entropy loss for each class, averaged

4.5. Technical details 
Regarding architecture, the model was built to work with 256 × 256 
images, which is enough to fit most of the game sprites. For both tasks, 
the input has 3 channels. For shading and coloring, respectively, the 
output has 7 classes and up to 43 labels. Regarding deep supervision, 
both the input and outputs are down-sampled using 2D Average Pooling, 
while, within the network, down-sampling layers use the Max Pooling 
operation. Regarding up-sampling, we do not use transposed convolu­
tions. Instead, we rely on the Up Sampling layer with the nearest- 
neighbor interpolation. Finally, all convolutions are 3 × 3 with stride 
one, followed by batch normalization [52] and the ReLU activation 
function [51]. We do not employ dropout or weight decay. 
Regarding network size, each down/up-sampling stage uses f ∗72 
filters, being f equals to 1, 2, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, when down-sampling, and f 
equals to 8,8,8,8,4,2,1, when up-sampling. In total, the final model has 
X = 53, 791, 206 trainable parameters and y = 209 convolutions. 
All models were trained in mixed-precision mode using the RMSprop 
optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 for 200 epochs in batches of 8 
images. Augmentation-wise, we only used random horizontal flipping in 
all experiments. All experiments were done using the TensorFlow 2 
Keras API [53] on Windows using a single GTX 2070 GPU. Depending on 
the configuration, training a complete model from beginning to end 
takes from one to two hours, on average. Inference times are negligible. 
5. Tests and results 
In this section, we discuss the results obtained with our solution on 
Trajes Fatais: Suits of Fate’s pipeline. We subdivide this section as follows: 
a description of the dataset and evaluation metrics, overall results, 
ablation study and, finally, some potential threats to validity. 
5.1. Dataset description 
We bring out and discuss our model results for three game charac­
ters: Lucy, Sarah, and Saulo. Lucy is an adult woman wearing collant 
clothing, Sarah is a tiny girl with a big platypus suit, and Saulo is a young 
male wearing a scarecrow costume. Unlike in our previous work [15], all 
three characters are now fully drawn by the human artists, having 
respectively 602, 352, and 588 sprites, out of which 170, 94, and 164 are 
reserved as the validation set. Regarding colors, Lucy, Sarah, and Saulo 
use, respectively, 28, 37, and 30 distinct coloring tones. 
Among the game’s fifteen characters, we selected those based on 
their visual features. Lucy sprites work well as a baseline, being easy to 
shade and color, with most tones being equally frequent. Sarah has many 
large smooth surfaces that are easy to shade and color. However, the girl 
within the suit is often shadowed by the costume and has many infre­
quent color tones that can be hard to infer. Finally, Saulo presents a 
shading challenge, often going from the darkest to the brightest shading 
tones and back in a matter of pixels. Fig. 6 shows the distribution of 
shading tones, from darker to brighter, and color tones, from most to 
least frequent. 
5.2. Evaluation metrics 
To assess the algorithm efficacy, we employed two main metrics: 
accuracy and balanced accuracy. The former measures the number of 
correctly predicted pixels out of the total, without correcting for class 
imbalance. On the other hand, the latter takes into account the number 
of samples in each class. It is computed as the average recall among all 
classes. 
To evaluate the algorithm’s confusion, we also computed the top-k 
accuracy metric, with k = 3 and k = 5. This score evaluates if the correct 
class is among the k classes the algorithm is most confident for the given 
pixel. Therefore, when compared to the raw accuracy, this metric re­
veals the percentage of pixels that were almost classified correctly. 
Finally, after computing these metrics, we discarded the background 
class, which can easily dominate the results, as it is easily predictable 
and is by far the most frequent class. In summary, all presented results 
are relative to sprite pixels. 
5.3. Overall results 
Based on our validation set, we extracted a set of shading and col­
oring images generated by our algorithm, along with their respective 
ground truth (Fig. 7). To select these images, we converted the one-hot 
encoded outputs to the RGB color space and computed each sprite root- 
mean-squared error (RMSE) against the ground truth. Then, we sorted 
sprites by error, selecting six samples from each task for presentation. 
From bottom-to-top, the first sprite is the one with the least error and the 
last is the one with the most. We chose to select sprites by RMSE instead 
of accuracy as this score correlates well to how the human visual system 
perceives errors in images. Moreover, this avoids presentation bias, as 
the image were mechanically selected rather than chosen by hand. 
Regarding shading, all three characters present very good results, 
with most of the predicted shading correlating to the human drawn one. 
Zooming into each image, most of the inaccuracies tend to occur at the 
edges of shading transitions and, more specifically, along the highlight 
(the brightest white tone). Specific to each character, most of the inac­
curacies within Lucy sprites are at her hair and hands, around Sarah’s 
joints and clothes, and along Saulo’s face, torso and pants, being this last 
one the character with most errors. The highest error sprites (topmost 
row) all come from special attack animations, which usually employ 
weapons and challenging poses. Collectively, all these sprites, despite 
not being perfect, present many areas that could be used in the game as 
is or with little to no alteration. Moreover, many of the shading de­
viations are consistent with the sprite pose and could have been a human 
artist choice. 
Regarding color sprites, most deviations occur along region bound­
aries and around minor elements, such as the eyes and lips, while more 
representative regions, like the arms, legs and clothes, tend to be 
correctly predicted in most instances. As we move to the highest error 
sprites, most inaccuracies appear around infrequent elements, such as 
weapons or, in the Sarah case, along the girl, when she leaves the 
platypus suit. At the topmost row, the highest error sprite of each 
character also come from special attack animations, that call for chal­
lenging poses and, in Saulo’s case, calls for his crow companion. In a

converge fully. 
5.4. Ablation study 
In this section, we present the results we obtained when developing 
our current model. In more detail, we present the relative improvement 
obtained from each element we introduced in our solution, starting with 
the base U-Net model. To streamline our investigation, we constrained 
this section to the evaluation of Lucy color sprites. 
During our initial investigation, our main concern was to tackle the 
problems we found in our previous work, which were mainly on the 
coloring task [15]. For this, we kept our problem formulation as a pixel- 
to-pixel mapping problem, but we replaced the pixel-level task from a 
color regression problem to a full-fledged classification formulation, 
using one-hot encoded labels and the softmax activation function. This 
change directly addresses our issues with regressing color values for the 
coloring problem, which were challenging to quantize to the fixed set of 
tones used by each character. In Table 2, this new model corresponds to 
the first row of the table. 
From this point forward, our goal was to encourage improving the 
algorithm performance. However, this proved quite challenging. 
Instead, considering human evaluation, we shifted our attention to 
steering our solution’s errors to be less erroneous. For instance, it is 
better to mistake the leg tone with the feet than with an eye or lip. For 
that reason, we implemented deep supervision, with the goal of 
encouraging the algorithm to focus its attention on a limited set of 
classes on each region by also supervising at lower resolutions. This 
change is shown at the second row of Table 2 and provided a noticeable 
improvement on all metrics. Marginal improvements were also obtained 
by individually weighting each loss term (third row of Table 2). 
To further push the algorithm towards correctly classifying minority 
classes, we investigated the use of a class-weighted focal loss [19,20] 
(fourth and fifth rows of Table 2). These terms seek to even out class 
imbalance by re-weighting each class contribution to the final loss and 
by gradually assigning more attention to less confident predictions. In 
our experiments, they led to an additional percentage point in balanced 
accuracy, at the expense of some raw accuracy. We deem this trade-of 
worthy, as the accuracy we lost likely comes from majority classes 
while the gains we obtained come from less frequent labels. In practice, 
this means we traded more problematic errors for more forgiving ones. 
Finally, in an effort to study if adding more depth to the network 
would yield additional benefit, we resorted to dense connections 
[17,18]. We chose this approach as it allows us to increase depth 
without compromising GPU resources. In practice, this regained most of 
the lost raw accuracy while also boosting our balanced one (last row of 
Table 2). However, these gains came at a cost. While the model shrinked 
almost ten million parameters, its memory use and execution time 
nearly doubled, due to the increased number of layers, slowing down 
iteration times considerably. 
5.5. Threats to validity 
So far, we have concerned ourselves with the specific problems of 
Trajes Fatais: Suits of Fate’s pipeline, namely the problems of shading and 
coloring sprites. In our scenario, every character has a minimum of 300 
sprites, with the average being 507. While this number is quite small in 
contrast to other problems [11,26], the majority of games use consid­
erably less sprites per character, specially outside the fighting genre. 
This puts most game-related problems in the realm of few-shot learning 
[51] and, hence, our approach might not work or be the most sensible 
path of action. Additionally, the segmentation formulation might not be 
the most sensible approach for problems with a large number of output 
classes (e.g., 50 or more). Moreover, while it is not unusual for

6. Conclusion and future work 
In this work, we investigated the use of deep learning algorithms to 
create pixel art sprites from line art sketches to produce artwork that is 
of sufficient quality to be used within a game with little to no manual 
editing from human artists. More specifically, we set this work within 
the Trajes Fatais: Suits of Fate pipeline, which consists of drawing shading 
and coloring sprites from line-art sketches. This work extends our pre­
vious research [15] on the topic with a vastly improved model, 
embracing the problem as a pixel-wise classification task without 
adversarial training and presenting significantly improved results for 
both shading and coloring tasks. Ultimately, this work demonstrates 
positive evidence that the current image generation state-of-the-art is 
ready to be used in game-related tasks, especially within problems that 
lack large datasets, deviate considerably from natural images, and are 
extremely intolerant to errors and artifacts of any kind. 
Future studies can follow at least three potential research directions: 
(1) further use cases of image generation within game pipelines, (2) the 
design of AI-assisted production schemes, and (3) enhancing the neural 
network design for improved sprite generation. In more detail, some 
worth exploring use cases of image generation in games are: to create in- 
between frames, to blend sprites, game style transfer, style-preserving 
rescaling routines, among others. Regarding AI-assisted pipelines, it is 
worth exploring how to leverage even smaller datasets, such as incom­
plete characters, and how to train such models incrementally using 
active learning and data-centric techniques [51]. Finally, there is plenty 
of room to improve the current neural network design. These are 
perceptual losses [54,55], the attention mechanism [44], and additional 
artistic control elements [11]. 
Finally, machine learning is showing promising footholds in creative 
art and making it more accessible. Nevertheless, despite its fundamental 
relevance, we believe that it will never completely wipe out the tradi­
tional forms of artistic creativity. On the contrary, we believe machines 
have the ultimate potential to unlock our most creative selves.
